title: Derivations-on-k-algebras 2026-07-25
content:
The definition of derivations on a commutative \(k\)-algebra \(A\) is the generalization from the concept
of derivations on the linear space \(\mathscr{C} (M)\) consisting of the smooth
functions on the manifold \(M\), which
are equivalently the smooth vector fields on \(M\), denoted as \(\mathfrak{X} (M) = \Gamma (\mathrm{T}
M)\).

Definition Given a commutative \(k\)-algebra \(A\) where \(k\) is a field (or a commutative ring), we
define a subset of \(\operatorname{End}_k
(A)\),
\[
\operatorname{Deri}_k (A) \triangleq \{ f \in
   \operatorname{End}_k (A) | \forall x, y \in A, f (x y) = f (x)
   y + x f (y) \}
\]
called the space of derivations on \(A\). The property \(f (x y) = f (x) y + x f (y)\) is called the
Leibniz law. \(\operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\) is itself a
\(k\)-linear space (or a \(k\)-module), since the following
formulas
\[
\begin{align*}
  (f + g) (x) & \triangleq f (x) + g (x)\\
  (a f) (x) & \triangleq a f (x)
\end{align*}
\]
define the addition and the scalar multiplication of \(\operatorname{Deri}_k\). It is direct to
check that both \(f + g\) and \(a f\) are still in the set \(\operatorname{Deri}_k\), which ensures the
closedness of linear operations on \(\operatorname{Deri}_k\).
\(\blacksquare\)
However, \(\operatorname{Deri}_k
(A)\) is not itself a \(k\)-algebra, regarding the fact that
compositing 2 derivations \(f\) and
\(g\) on \(A\) does not result in another new
derivation \(f g \in \operatorname{End}_k (A)
\supsetneqq \operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\) in general. To see this,
consider the example that \(A =\mathscr{C}_p
(M)\) for some \(p \in M\) and
\(f = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, g =
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\), with \(i \neq j\). The composition of \(f\) and \(g\) is \(f g =
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^i \partial x^j}\), which is not a
derivation, since it does not satisfy that \(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^i \partial x^j}
(\varphi \psi) = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^i \partial x^j} (\varphi)
\psi + \varphi \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^i \partial x^j}
(\psi)\). So composition of 2 derivations is usually not a
derivation.
But we can define such an algebraic operation on \(\operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\), called the
commutator.
Theorem For any pair of derivations \(f, g \in \operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\), the
commutator of \(f\) and \(g\)
\[[f, g] \triangleq f g - g f
\]
is a derivation. Since \(\operatorname{End}_k (A)\) is a \(k\)-algebra, it is closed under
multiplication and subtraction. So \(f g - g f
\in \operatorname{End}_k (A)\). The theorem says that, the
commutator \([f, g]\) of \(f\) and \(g\) is also in \(\operatorname{Deri}_k (A) \subseteq
\operatorname{End}_k (A)\).
Proof
To prove that \(h = f g - g f \in
\operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\), we only need to check the Leibniz’s
law. To check this, we consider
\[
\begin{align*}
  h (x y) = & (f g - g f) (x y)\\
  = & (f g) (x y) - (g f) (x y)\\
  = & f (g (x y)) - g (f (x y))\\
  = & f (g (x) y + x g (y)) - g (f (x) y + x f (y))\\
  = & f (g (x) y) + f (x g (y)) - g (f (x) y) - g (x f (y))\\
  = & f (g (x)) y + g (x) f (y) + f (x) g (y) + x f (g (y))\\
  & - g (f (x)) y - f (x) g (y) - g (x) f (y) - x g (f (y))\\
  = & (f g - g f) (x) y + x (f g - g f) (y)\\
  = & h (x) y + x h (y)
\end{align*}
\]
Therefore, \(h\) satisfies the
Leibniz law, and thus \(h \in
\operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\).
\(\Box\)
Note that in the formulas above, the terms \(f (x) g (y)\) and \(g (x) f (y)\) are both cancelled.
Furthermore, these terms are related to the Poisson
bracket of \(x\) and \(y\).
Definition Given 2 derivations \(f\) and \(g\) on the \(k\)-algebra \(A\), the Poisson bracket
of 2 elements \(x, y \in A\) with
respect to \(f, g\) is defined as
\[\{ x, y \}_{f, g} = f (x) g (y) - g (x)
f (y) \]
\(\blacksquare\)
The Poisson brackets are closely related to the commutators. In
canonical quantization in quantum mechanics, the Poisson bracket of the
classical quantities are replaced by the commutator where quantities are
changed to operators.
Thus we have a different algebraic operator on \(\operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\), where \(\operatorname{End}_k (A)\) is the algebra
with operator being the composition of linear mappings, and \(\operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\) is the algebra
with operator being the commutator of derivations.
This space of derivations \(\operatorname{Deri}_k (A)\), together with
the commutator, is an example of a Lie algebra.
